paras: The expulsion order against Black women in Spokane's "burnt district" was a September 1903 attempt by the Spokane, Washington, police to drive ten Black women out of the city's crib alleys and out of town. Women who refused to leave were arrested and fined for vagrancy, but their attorney charged the police with racial discrimination, and within a week the police commissioner told the chief not to repeat it. The Spokane Press followed the case for a week and returned to it in November.

The women worked in Nome and Klondike alleys, the crib district of the "burnt district," where, according to their attorney, each paid a monthly fine to the city as the white women of the district did. The Spokane Press described the chief's move as a "crusade against the worst women" of the district and reported that a later order would be aimed at the "dead tough" white women.

On Saturday, September 19, Chief of Police Woydt ordered ten Black women to leave the alleys and the town. Four of them, Ruth Simms, Mabel Roberts, Grace Williams and Victoria Smith, refused and were arrested for vagrancy the next night; Lizzie Morgan, Beatrice Kennedy, Ollie James, Hattie Harding and Pauline Edwards were also named among those ordered out. The paper added that each woman would be "repeatedly arrested and fined" unless she left Spokane.

Attorney N. E. Nuzum appeared for the women in police court on September 21, where Justice Hinkle fixed bond at $15 each. By the next day the paper spoke of all ten as arrested; each pleaded not guilty, and on September 23 each was fined for vagrancy over Nuzum's protests. The police gave as their reason that the women were "inveterate thieves" whose offenses could not be proved for lack of evidence.

Nuzum answered by serving notice on Prosecuting Attorney Horace Kimball, Sheriff W. J. Doust and Constable Fred Baling that 80 named women were running houses of prostitution, and he threatened to prosecute any official who did not act. Kimball and Baling said they would take no action, Kimball calling it a city matter, while Doust said he would seek legal advice. On September 24 eight of the ten women were released on bail, and they had not been re-arrested by the next day.

Police Commissioner Root then asked Chief Woydt not to discriminate in this way again and said the women were to have equal rights with white women of their class, and ten notices that had been prepared were reportedly not served. The same issue reported that Wanda Lewis, a Black woman from Lewiston, Idaho, had arranged for nine of the ten to go with her to Lewiston, whose police chief threatened to arrest them on arrival, while Nuzum said some of the women were not leaving town. No later report says whether any of the women left; in November the Spokane Press said the prosecutions had been stopped and the police called off.

All known coverage comes from the Spokane Press, which ran the story on its front page on September 21, 22, 24, 25 and 26. Its headlines ran from "TOUGH WOMEN CRUSADE" to "DUSKY BELLES TO HIKE," and it printed the police's theft charge without comment. At the same time it quoted Nuzum at length, including his statement that the police meant "to run out the negro women" by "rank persecution," and it reported the commissioner's rebuke of the chief.

In a November column on vice politics the paper went further, calling the crime charge the police's ostensible ground and linking the campaign to a scheme to give a Post street landlady a monopoly. No account of the episode was found in the Black press or in any other white paper.

The reports differ on the number arrested, with the first item counting four and later items treating all ten as arrested. They also leave the outcome unclear: the September 24 report has all ten fined, the next day's report has eight released on bail, and the November column says the prosecutions were stopped. The police's account of the women as thieves came only from the police, while the charge of racial discrimination came from the women's attorney.

accounts.label: Police
accounts.gist: The police said the women were inveterate thieves guilty of countless acts for which evidence to convict could not be found, and the first report presented the order as the start of a crusade against the worst women of the district.

accounts.label: Women's attorney
accounts.gist: Nuzum said the women were being driven out only because they were Black, that each had paid her monthly fine like the white women, and that none had been convicted of anything but her trade.

accounts.label: Spokane Press retrospective
accounts.gist: In November the paper said the crime charge was ostensible and tied the campaign to a scheme to give a Post street landlady a monopoly, adding that Nuzum's threats stopped the prosecutions.
